This morning, the light over Cambridge had that gentle, honeyed quality that makes even the most hurried cyclist slow their pace. As I sat at my desk, preparing notes for my lecture on the social reformers of the late 19th century, my gaze kept drifting to the row of small pots along the windowsill. Each succulent, in its own peculiar shape, seemed a quiet custodian of time — steady, enduring, and untroubled by the shifting seasons outside. I've never been much for flower beds; perhaps it’s the historian in me, drawn to what persists rather than what blooms briefly. The streets below stirred with early chatter, coffee cups in hand, as I thought about the quiet contributions forgotten in textbooks. Like my plants, these figures survive in the margins, awaiting recognition.

This morning, the light over Cambridge carried that gentle, honeyed quality that can coax even the most hurried cyclist into a more leisurely ride. Seated at my desk, sorting through notes for a lecture on late 19th‑century social reformers, I found my gaze wandering to the line of small pots along the windowsill. Each succulent, with its singular geometry, stood like a quiet custodian of time — resilient, unhurried, and unconcerned with the changing seasons beyond the glass. I've never taken to flower beds; perhaps the historian in me leans towards what endures rather than what dazzles briefly. From the street below drifted the soft hum of morning conversations, the clink of coffee cups, and I thought about the quiet contributors history consigns to the margins — steady presences, awaiting their recognition.
